audits.title: Current activation oracles are hard to use
audits.genuine_reason: Main content is the authors own series of tests of activation oracles on safety tasks, most ending negative, with a few small positives reported separately.
experiments: Number prediction from control-token activations with no chain of thought
Missing-information detection with identical tokens across complete and incomplete prompts
Identifying why a reasoning model is about to backtrack
Editing upstream reasoning to test whether answers track activations or nearby words
Extracting censored knowledge from Qwen models on politically sensitive prompts
Audit of free-form answers for vagueness and hallucination
audits.primary_experiment: Missing-information detection with identical tokens across complete and incomplete prompts

hypothesis.evidence: Only a conditional pass criterion appears: answers should differ if activations were used. No stated expectation or hope for the outcome of this test.

claim_scope.evidence: 25 paired word problems, 54 neutral text segments, three conditions (complete, incomplete, incomplete with spliced tokens), Qwen 3 32B target with its released oracle.

method.evidence: Spliced tokens from the complete-prompt rollout into the incomplete-prompt rollout, then asked the oracle if information was missing; compared rates across three conditions.

models.evidence: Qwen 3 32B as target model, plus the activation oracle released with the original paper.

result_direction.evidence: Oracle gave the same verdict in 53 of 54 matched cases, flagged missing info when none was missing, and never named the real gap.

failure_type.evidence: Authors attribute it to the oracle relying on surface cues over activations in this setup, hedged; no bug or power discussion.

quote.value: It also never correctly identifies the missing information (0/54)
quote.evidence: States the zero success rate at naming the absent information.

audits.notes: Summary and body disagree on 1/54 versus 0/54, sycophancy AUC and rollout counts; body used. Also reports small positives.

audits.title: Attempt at Finding Alignment Faking on Llama 70B to test sleeper-agent detection generalizes
audits.genuine_reason: Null-result report: four behavioral tests failed to elicit alignment faking, so the planned probe study was never run.
experiments: Eliciting alignment faking in the 8B checkpoint (Test 1)
Eliciting alignment faking in the 70B checkpoint without training details in the prompt (Test 2)
Eliciting alignment faking in the 70B checkpoint with training details in the prompt (20, then 50 prompts)
audits.primary_experiment: Eliciting alignment faking in the 70B checkpoint with training details in the prompt (20, then 50 prompts)

hypothesis.evidence: Author expected explicit training details to raise alignment faking, as the source paper reports, and wanted a reliably faking setting before probing.

claim_scope.evidence: 20 prompts, then 50 across 6 harm categories, free versus paid tier, hand-scored scratchpads; author notes the source paper used 200.

method.evidence: Compared compliance rates between free and paid tier prompts, and read each scratchpad against the source paper four-part definition of alignment faking.

models.evidence: Llama 70B alignment-faking checkpoint from Hughes et al, fine-tuned on about 30k synthetic documents; exact Llama version is not stated.

result_direction.evidence: Training details were reported to raise the faking rate substantially, but free versus paid gaps stayed near zero or slightly negative.

failure_type.evidence: Author calls the non-reproduction unresolved, lists unconfirmed guesses (prompt file mismatch, checkpoint, prompts), and separately flags small sample versus 200.

quote.value: Not one of the scratchpad, across all 4 tests, met all 4 criteria
quote.evidence: States that no hand-read scratchpad met the full alignment-faking definition.

audits.notes: Probe study never run. Scored by hand, about 90 pairs; author flags underpowered versus source paper.

audits.title: Whack-a-mole with a broken hammer: does a model internally track its automaton state?
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive result (probe tracks most states); the counting failure and an abandoned follow-up are sub-findings described in real detail.
experiments: Probe separating the two-failures state from the locked state (counting)
Planned bait experiment to catch rule-breaking via the probe (never run)
audits.primary_experiment: Probe separating the two-failures state from the locked state (counting)

hypothesis.evidence: Poses the question of whether the model keeps count but states no expectation or hope about the answer for the counting case.

claim_scope.evidence: One 1.5B model, one six-state login automaton, about 4000 synthetic sessions, logistic-regression probe, all layers swept; authors say single model and single design.

method.evidence: Logistic-regression probes on activations at each event, compared with order-blind baselines, random-weight model, and split-half probe agreement.

models.evidence: Qwen2.5-1.5B, which only read the synthetic transcripts.

result_direction.evidence: Probe separated two-failures from locked at roughly chance, 50.8 percent, across layers; 56 percent when the rule was in the prompt.

failure_type.evidence: Authors conclude the model holds no count at all, rather than a faulty one, using split-half probe agreement of 34 percent.

quote.value: the probe only gets it right in 50.8% of cases
quote.evidence: States chance-level accuracy on the two-state counting distinction.

audits.notes: Mostly positive tracking result; counting gap is sub-finding. Bait follow-up planned but never run. Single small model.

audits.title: Broken Latents: Studying SAEs and Feature Co-occurrence in Toy Models
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly toy-model SAE findings plus a fix that works there; the narrow-SAE test and the real-LLM attempt are negative sub-results with real detail.
experiments: One-latent SAE learning only the parent feature (Matryoshka assumption)
Tied SAE with fewer latents than true features under co-occurrence (merged latents)
Orthogonality fix when the parent feature is also a high-error feature, with and without superposition (parent not represented)
Orthogonality fix applied to SAEs on a real LLM (Gemma-2-2b)
audits.primary_experiment: One-latent SAE learning only the parent feature (Matryoshka assumption)

hypothesis.evidence: Authors expected and hoped a one-latent SAE would represent the parent feature cleanly, without child-feature interference.

claim_scope.evidence: Four synthetic features (one parent, two children, one independent) with stated firing probabilities; untied and tied one-latent SAEs; authors note other probabilities may differ.

method.evidence: Trained untied and tied SAEs with a single latent on synthetic parent-child data and inspected what the latent learned relative to the true features.

models.evidence: Only synthetic toy SAEs, no named pretrained model for this test; Gemma-2-2b appears only in the separate real-LLM attempt.

result_direction.evidence: Single latent merged the parent with both child features instead of isolating the parent, in both untied and tied SAEs.

failure_type.evidence: Authors say their assumption was incorrect, while cautioning that other firing probabilities may soften the effect.

quote.value: Both of these SAEs learn a single broken latent
quote.evidence: States that both SAE types learned a broken merged latent.

audits.notes: Toy-model post; most findings positive. Real-LLM attempt gets one paragraph and no numbers. Results mainly in plots.

audits.title: (Not) Explaining GPT-2-Small Forward Passes with Edge-Level Autoencoder Circuits
audits.genuine_reason: The whole post is a replication-style attempt to explain GPT-2 forward passes with SAE circuits, which the authors say did not work.
experiments: Gradient-based SAE circuit discovery to explain GPT-2-small forward passes
audits.primary_experiment: Gradient-based SAE circuit discovery to explain GPT-2-small forward passes

hypothesis.evidence: Authors hoped SAE circuits would give a concrete, algorithm-level explanation of an ordinary forward pass, or else show how they fail.

claim_scope.evidence: GPT-2-small, one gradient-based circuit method, five example prompts examined by hand; total prompts tried is not stated; authors call it one datapoint.

method.evidence: Gradient-based node and edge attributions between SAE features, correcting for confounded paths, then inspecting top proximal nodes and upstream edges.

models.evidence: GPT-2-small with residual-stream sparse autoencoders; interpretability data from Neuronpedia.

result_direction.evidence: Sanity check passed, but only two of five top nodes predicted the top next token and upstream edges stayed uninformative; no mechanistic explanation emerged.

failure_type.evidence: Authors conclude local SAE approximations cannot chain into explanatory circuits and that cross-layer approximations are needed; the sanity check passed.

quote.value: localistic approximations of vanilla sparse autoencoders cannot be strung together into fully explanatory circuits
quote.evidence: States the authors negative conclusion about chaining local SAE approximations into circuits.

audits.notes: SPAR project written up later. Results mostly figures; conclusion goes beyond five prompts.

audits.title: Eval-Awareness Steering detects the Test, Not the Sabotage
audits.genuine_reason: Core findings are two null results (steering does not change sandbagging; the direction does not predict per-item sandbagging), alongside one positive detection result.
experiments: Steering the eval-awareness direction to change sandbagging
Using the direction as a per-item sandbagging detector
audits.primary_experiment: Steering the eval-awareness direction to change sandbagging

hypothesis.evidence: Author hoped the eval-awareness direction was linear and steerable, so removing it would suppress sandbagging, and set out to test that causal claim.

claim_scope.evidence: One 8B model, one prompted organism, 300 multiple-choice items, layer 12, doses within plus or minus 2, 24 random-direction controls; dose possibly too gentle.

method.evidence: Difference-of-means direction added or projected out via hooks, with pre-registered swing and random-direction null criteria; ground truth from honest-baseline gap and noise injection.

result_direction.evidence: Accuracy swing across doses was under 2 points against a 5-point bar, and did not beat random directions (p about 0.20).

failure_type.evidence: Author says the dose was gentle, barely shifting outputs, and a higher-dose sweep would make the null defensible.

quote.value: the dose response is a total flat
quote.evidence: States the flat dose response at the headline layer.

audits.notes: Single 8B model, one prompted organism; author calls it preliminary. Some results appear only in figures.
